structure.overview: This case is a judicial review of an IRCC Officer's decision refusing the Applicant's permanent residence application under the Canadian Experience Class due to self-employed work experience, which is excluded by the Regulations. The Applicant, a 28-year-old Indian citizen, argued the decision was unreasonable and unfair, while the Respondent maintained there was no reviewable error. The court found the Officer's decision reasonable and dismissed the application.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: This is a judicial review application of an IRCC Officer's decision refusing permanent residence under Canadian Experience Class due to self-employed work experience.

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27, s 72(1)
Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227, s 87(1)

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant is a 28-year-old Indian citizen who applied for permanent residence under the Canadian Experience Class in November 2022.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The Applicant claimed Canadian work experience from April 2021 with a numbered company, which was self-employed work excluded by the Regulations.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant raises issues about reviewable errors in the Officer's refusal decision and its reasonableness.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Respondent submits the Applicant failed to show any reviewable error in the Officer's decision.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court states the main issue is whether the Officer's decision is reasonable.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer's Procedural Fairness Letter raised concerns about the Applicant's job duties, employment location, and low salary inconsistent with the executive director role.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant replied that she performed substantial duties, location does not disqualify, no minimum wage applies, and she meets Federal Skilled Worker Class requirements.

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, ss 75(1) and 75(2)
citations.why: Applicant cites Federal Skilled Worker Class requirements

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer's Decision states the Applicant's work experience was self-employed under exemption code C11, which does not qualify for Canadian Experience Class.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Officer refused the Applicant's permanent residence application under IRPA subsections 10.3(1)(e) and 11.2.

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, ss 10.3(1)(e) and 11.2

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Regulations at s 87.1(2) set out Canadian Experience Class membership requirements including one year of full-time work in specified occupations with substantial duties.

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, s 87.1(2)
citations.why: sets membership requirements for Canadian Experience Class

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Regulations s 87.1(3) excludes self-employment and unauthorized work from qualifying work experience.

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, s 87.1(3)
citations.why: excludes self-employment from qualifying work experience

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: IRPA s 11.2 prohibits issuing permanent residence documents if criteria under s 10.3(1)(e) are not met.

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, s 11.2
citations.why: legal provision preventing issuance if criteria unmet

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The parties agree the standard of review is reasonableness; procedural fairness is reviewed on correctness per Vavilov at para 23.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, [2019] 4 SCR 653, para 23
citations.why: sets standards for reasonableness and procedural fairness review

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Canada Post Corp v Canadian Union of Postal Workers explains what constitutes a reasonable decision and court's role in reasonableness review.

citations.cite: Canada Post Corp v Canadian Union of Postal Workers, 2019 SCC 67
citations.why: explains reasonableness standard and court's review role

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant argues the Decision is unreasonable and unfair for ignoring work experience under work permit exception code C11 and overlooking evidence.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant submits the Decision did not address concerns raised in the Procedural Fairness Letter and repeats her prior arguments.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds the core fact is self-employed work, which is excluded by s 87.1(3)(b), making the Decision reasonable and the only reasonable conclusion.

citations.cite: Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, s 87.1(3)(b)
citations.why: self-employment excluded from qualifying work experience

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Officer had no duty to inform the Applicant about the self-employment exclusion as it is public legislation and obvious; no judicial intervention warranted.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court rejects the Applicant's fettering argument, noting fettering does not apply to legislated criteria like these Regulations.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant's argument for consideration under Federal Skilled Worker Class lacks merit as she was not invited or applied under that Class.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court concludes the application must be dismissed.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: A reasonable decision is coherent, rational, justified by facts and law, and courts must review reasons with respectful attention per Vavilov.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, para 85
citations.why: defines reasonableness as coherent and justified decision

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, para 84
citations.why: court must review reasons with respectful attention

citations.cite: Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, para 48
citations.why: quoted in Vavilov on reviewing reasons

citations.cite: Newfoundland Nurses' Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Reasonableness depends on legal and factual context; decision must show justification, transparency, and intelligibility per Vavilov.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, para 90
Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, para 99
citations.why: decision must show justification, transparency, intelligibility

citations.cite: Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, paras 47 and 74
Catalyst Paper Corp. v. North Cowichan (District), 2012 SCC 2, para 13

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The party challenging a decision bears the burden to show the decision is unreasonable due to central or significant flaws per Vavilov.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, para 100
citations.why: burden on challenger to prove unreasonableness
